mainEntity.name: Do you provide specialty clinic cleaning in Charlton, MA?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Charlton (Worcester County) is one of the 109 Massachusetts cities and towns we serve. It is about 26 miles southwest of our Marlborough base in a straight line. Every engagement starts with a free on-site assessment; call (978) 307-8107.

mainEntity.name: Which Charlton ZIP codes do you cover?

acceptedAnswer.text: All of them: 01507. If your facility sits on a town line, tell us the street address and we will confirm.

mainEntity.name: Which nearby towns do you also serve?

acceptedAnswer.text: The closest served towns to Charlton are Oxford (about 5.2 mi), Dudley (about 5.8 mi), Auburn (about 7.7 mi). See the full list on our service areas page.

mainEntity.name: Half our equipment sits in a gray zone where nobody is sure who cleans it. How do you fix that?

acceptedAnswer.text: With a written responsibility matrix built device by device before we start. Every surface and device in the suite gets an owner, a product, a method, and a frequency. In Massachusetts this is not discretionary housekeeping: 105 CMR 140.211(B) requires diagnostic and therapeutic equipment to be disinfected after each use in accordance with recognized standards of practice, and that duty sits with the licensed clinic. Our job is to take the surfaces that can safely be ours and to make the remainder explicitly, visibly, and in writing someone else's.

mainEntity.name: Can you handle disinfection of our probes and scopes?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Semi-critical items, meaning anything that contacts mucous membranes or non-intact skin, require at least high-level disinfection after thorough pre-cleaning, per the CDC Infection Prevention Checklist for Outpatient Settings, High-Level Disinfection items A through C. That is a trained clinical reprocessing function with its own competency validation, test strips, and logs. A surface wipe on a semi-critical probe is a survey finding, not a shortcut. We clean the reprocessing room around it: counters, sinks, floors, and the physical separation between the dirty end and the clean end.

mainEntity.name: Do you need your own storage space in our suite?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and Massachusetts effectively requires it. 105 CMR 140.206 requires cleaning compounds to be clearly labeled and stored in a locked utility closet, with a service sink supplied with hot and cold water for filling and emptying housekeeping equipment. Our chemicals stay labeled, secured, and out of patient areas, and mop water is never emptied into a clinical or handwashing sink. If your suite has no compliant utility closet, that appears in our walkthrough report, because it is a licensure exposure before it is a cleaning inconvenience.

Inside a Charlton service visit

High-touch surfaces on every visit

  • Keyboards and imaging workstation surfaces
  • Patient positioning aids
  • Door handles and light switches
  • Check-in counter and payment terminal
  • Waiting-room seating
  • Restroom fixtures

How a visit runs

  1. Map each room's specialty equipment and agree which surfaces the clinical team reprocesses per the manufacturer's instructions.
  2. Clean environmental surfaces around the equipment with products compatible with its finishes.
  3. Clean before disinfecting where surfaces are visibly soiled, then hold the label contact time.
  4. Keep procedure rooms on their own cloths and equipment, cleaned last in the room order.
  5. Damp-mop floors, including under procedure chairs.

A starting schedule

  • Exam and consult rooms: daily.
  • Waiting areas and restrooms: daily, more often in high-volume clinics.
  • Floors: daily.

Clinics that share space with other practices need the cleaning scope drawn along suite lines.

Documentation you receive

  • Room and equipment-area checklist
  • Product list with EPA registration numbers and contact times
  • Safety Data Sheets
  • Signed service logs

Survey findings we help Charlton facilities prevent

Real, published regulatory findings — every citation links to its source.

CDC Infection Prevention Checklist, non-critical item definition; CDC Core Practices 5f

Shared non-critical devices used across a procedure day — blood pressure cuffs, chin rests, headrests, positioning equipment — not cleaned and disinfected between patients according to the degree of contamination.

CDC Infection Prevention Checklist for Outpatient Settings, Section II items A and B

Frequently touched surfaces in the procedure room not cleaned and then disinfected, and products not used to the manufacturer's dilution, storage, shelf-life and contact time.

29 CFR 1910.1030(d)(4)(i) and (d)(4)(ii)(A)

No written schedule for cleaning and decontamination, and contaminated work surfaces not decontaminated after procedures, after spills, and at end of shift.

Federal OSHA cited 29 CFR 1910.1030 three times in one inspection of other health practitioners' offices between October 2024 and September 2025 — the most-cited standard for that sector.

  • Which of our equipment surfaces will you clean, and which will you leave to our staff?
  • Are your products compatible with our equipment manufacturers' cleaning instructions?
  • What documentation will you leave after each visit?

We answer each of these in writing after the free assessment.
